extracted.intended_audience: psychologists, anthropologists, and scientifically-minded readers interested in mental imagery and memory
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and evaluating the qualities, variations, and functional significance of the human visualising (mental imagery) faculty, including number-forms, vividness, spatial properties, heredity, cultural differences, and trainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness/clarity of visual memory
rubrics_metrics.description: The clearness and vividness with which mental images appear; 'Images usually do not become stronger by dwelling on them; the first idea is commonly the most vigorous.' Some persons see images as if 'before their eyes' with objectivity comparable to reality, others scarcely at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include persons who mentally read off scores or manuscripts, and extremes range from inability to visualise anything to imagery so strong as to produce hallucinations. Note that vividness may be selective (e.g., form but not colour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from optical acuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharp sight is not necessarily accompanied by clear visual memory; the two faculties can be independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author reports multiple cases showing independence; do not assume good eyesight implies strong visual imagery when assessing subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to dreaming
rubrics_metrics.description: The visualising faculty does not inevitably correlate with dreaming; strong waking imagery can coexist with rare or faint dreams, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit questioning about dream vividness when profiling imagery — absence of dreams does not imply weak visualising power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic 'reading off' or replay of previously perceived texts/score
rubrics_metrics.description: Some persons mentally read every word that is uttered or replay musical scores; they attend to the visual equivalent rather than the sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether subjects report visual replay of manuscripts or music and whether this interferes with or aids performance (e.g., a statesman puzzled by image of manuscript during speech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness / stereoscopic and multi-aspect imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to combine in a single perception more than can be seen at one instant by the two eyes — e.g., visualising all sides of a solid body simultaneously or 'embracing an entire sphere in a single perception.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for reports of 'touch-sight' or the capacity to visualise objects nearly or entirely around; common in some specialists (mineralogists) and occurs in dreams/nightmares for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect methods for achieving comprehensive imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Many attain the effect of seeing whole objects or rooms by mental tactics: sweeping the scene, imagining transparency, or visualising themselves as actors on a mental stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct simultaneous imagery is absent, probe whether subjects use these strategies (transparent walls, distant viewpoint, mental stage) to achieve holistic visualisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial locus and projection of images
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the image appears in the mental field varies: in front of the eye, at a realistic distance, 'in a dark gray atmosphere', or other positions; some can project the image onto paper and hold it fast sufficiently to outline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the reported apparent distance and direction of images; the rare ability to project onto paper is testable (ask subject to outline mental image).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence/retention of retinal picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to retain a retinal picture after a brief flash, allowing subsequent analysis of details missed during the initial exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test via flashed scenes and retrospective description to evaluate retinal persistence; this is an easily developed faculty according to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical orientation tendency in imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mental images (localities) are inseparably connected with a sense of their position relative to compass points; strong geographical tendency allied to geographical comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe whether recalled localities include consistent compass orientation or positional sense; may correlate with mapping skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex and age differences
rubrics_metrics.description: The visualising faculty is reported higher in the female sex than in the male and somewhat higher in public schoolboys than men; advancing age often does not dim the faculty and may increase it, though abstract thinking in later life can impair it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sampling populations, stratify by sex and age and consider educational/abstract-thinking confounds when interpreting differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of education and book-learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Language and book-learning tend to dull the visualising faculty; 'our bookish and wordy education tends to repress this valuable gift of nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for educational background; those heavily trained in abstract symbolic thought (philosophers) often suppress imagery deliberately and may show weaker spontaneous visualising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heritability and familial clustering
rubrics_metrics.description: The visualising faculty is a natural gift with a tendency to be inherited; certain peculiarities are 'usually found among two, three, or more brothers and sisters, parents, children, uncles and aunts, and cousins.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect family histories and look for clustering beyond what education/family tradition would predict; author cites abundant evidence of heredity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racial and cultural differences (ethnographic evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some races and cultures show strong visualising powers (e.g., French, Bushmen, Eskimo), evidenced by prearranged ceremonials, skilled carving, map-drawing, and realistic self-taught illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ethnographic examples cautiously; control for effects of education, technology, and lifestyle when comparing populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trainability and education to strengthen imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The visualising faculty admits of being developed by education and practice; example: M. Lecoq de Boisbaudran's École Nationale de Dessein method strengthened pupils' sight-memory through study, tracing outlines with a pencil, and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training programs (study from models, associating sight with muscular memory, repeated practice) can markedly improve visual memory — include pre/post measures when evaluating training effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness in practical and professional contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Visualising is highly useful in mechanicians, engineers, architects, artists, strategists, and all who design; 'the best workmen are those who visualise the whole of what they propose to do before they take a tool in their hands.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing vocational aptitude or justifying training, measure imagery capacity as it relates to design and spatial planning tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of associations (multisensory and logical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplying associations strengthens visual memory; 'the healthiest memory being that in which all the associations are logical, and toward which all the senses concur in their due proportions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess multisensory associative strategies (looking at outside of house to recall inside) and encourage multimodal encoding in training for improved vividness and recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility vs tenacity of mental images
rubrics_metrics.description: Many persons show absence of flexibility: the first image holds tenaciously and is difficult to shift or reorient; others have complete mastery and can manipulate images at will (rotate, scale, animate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between subjects who form 'composite blurs' when images from many views combine and those who can dissect and manipulate components; test by asking for mental rotation, scaling, or re-presentation tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for generalised vs specific imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly reflective/intellectual persons may suppress specific imagery to hold the mind in suspense and produce generic images; the ability to form generic images from many experiences is valuable in higher thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe whether subjects produce specific detailed tableaux or generalised schematic images when given abstract nouns (e.g., 'boat'); this relates to philosophical/abstract thinking styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number-forms phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinct class of visual imagery in which numerals appear automatically in a vivid and invariable 'Form' in the mental field, each numeral occupying a definite place — the Form may be a line, rows, or shaded space and is nearly invariable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify presence/absence of number-forms by asking subjects to think of numerals and describe spatial arrangement, direction, distance, and invariance; author estimates frequency ~1 in 30 adult males or 1 in 15 females.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of number-forms: invariance, involuntariness, and individual pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Number-forms come into view independently of the will, their shape/position are nearly invariable, and patterns vary widely across individuals (angles, curves, panoramic extent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reproducibility over time (author obtained repeated sketches years apart that matched), familial occurrence, and whether the form extends to high numbers or becomes abstract beyond a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical corroboration and authenticity checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Trustworthiness of reports evaluated by independent corroboration: multiple correspondents, repeated sketches across years, family reports, and public demonstrations (Anthropological Institute meeting with diagrams).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When collecting self-reports, seek independent sketches, repeat assessments after intervals, and look for corroboration from relatives or other observers to validate reported imagery phenomena.
